activities.caption: pair each epic with its transmission predicament
activities.name: tcEpicMatch

config.prompt: Four classics, four predicaments — pair them:

pairs.right: fragments on clay tablets across the Near East — the twelfth tablet famously does not fit the narrative's logic
already an editorial battlefield in antiquity — suspect lines marked with obeli, and the tenth-century Venetus A an edition of editions
the Poona Critical Edition collated roughly 1,300 manuscripts — and regional traditions openly disagree with it
pure orality — performances compared as variants, Maas's method applied to living recitations

config.why: From Gilgamesh to Shakespeare, every classic arrives as a transmission problem — and the solutions differ: collation, critical editions, conflation, or fieldwork on oral performance.

activities.anchor: each with scenes the others lack
activities.caption: you are editing Hamlet — choose a policy, wear its consequences
activities.name: tcHamletBranch

config.root: No play manuscript in Shakespeare's hand survives. Hamlet exists in three distinct early versions — Q1 (1603, the 'bad quarto'), Q2 (1604–5, longer), and the Folio (1623) — each with material the others lack. Your editorial policy?

start.text: Three early Hamlets, one edition to build. What do you print?

choices.label: Conflate all three into one composite text
Treat the Folio as the theatrical text and Q2 as something else

composite.text: You have built a composite Hamlet Shakespeare never wrote — fluent, and false to the evidence. A conflated edition owes its readers an apparatus saying exactly what was merged.

versions.text: Three Hamlets, honestly printed — 'the text' becomes 'the texts', the corruption becomes the evidence, and your apparatus becomes very long.

oxford.text: The Folio as the theatrical text, Q2 as something else — a decision, not a discovery. The edition now argues a position about what kind of thing a play is.

config.why: 'The text' is a decision, everywhere — and editors must choose between conflating, printing separately, or re-describing the versions.

activities.caption: rebuild the editor's philosophy in order of pressure
activities.name: tcTheoryOrder

config.prompt: Editing is applied theory — put the positions in the order the argument moved:
items: The New Bibliography (Greg, Bowers): the author's final intention is the target; copy-text transmission is the obstacle
The 'intentional fallacy' (Wimsatt and Beardsley, 1946): if intention is unrecoverable, what is the editor reconstructing?
Structuralism and poststructuralism: if meaning is made by readers and the sign is unstable, the 'original' is a metaphysical preference, not a fact
The socialized text (McGann): every edition is a historically situated interpretation, documented in an apparatus
config.why: The variant, once corruption, became evidence — the honest edition documents its choices rather than hiding them behind W.

activities.anchor: The modern canon broke the editor's comfortable rules
activities.caption: find the line the editorial war refutes
activities.name: tcUlyssesSpot

config.prompt: One line of this modern-authorship report is wrong — click it:
lines: Yeats revised his poems across decades and stood by the late versions.
Dickinson left nearly 1,800 poem-variants, many assembled differently in her fascicles.
Kafka left instructions to burn his manuscripts.
The 1984 'Ulysses: The Corrected Text' settled 'which Ulysses?' for good.
Modern editing's answer is genetic: present the composition process, drafts to print, and let the work be plural.
config.correction: John Kidd's charges of construction errors made 'which Ulysses?' an open question — Gabler's synoptic edition triggered the fiercest editorial war of the century.
config.why: Postmodernism's question about origins suddenly had a concrete bibliography — and the version principle was institutionalised, not settled.

activities.caption: fill the blanks in The Trial's survival story
activities.name: tcBrodCloze

config.text: The unfinished manuscript survived only because %%0%% disobeyed the burn instruction — and the novel's chapter order is editorial reconstruction, since Kafka left his chapters %%1%% and partially unordered. Every German edition since %%2%% is an argument about a book its author declined to finish.
config.hint: The friend who disobeyed; what the chapters lacked; the year of the first printing.

activities.caption: file each version by the work it does
activities.name: tcTranslationBuckets

config.prompt: Translations multiply texts — file each by what it is:

items.label: the Septuagint's Greek, standing behind lost Hebrew readings
Aristotle reaching Europe through Syriac and Arabic — 'the' Aristotle descends from a round-trip
Schlegel's Romantic Hamlet for German readers
the retranslations that arrive roughly every generation as target languages shift

config.why: Each new translation creates a new tradition — and re-poses the question: which source text was the translator even translating?

activities.caption: drag the divider — what the date measures, and what it misses
activities.name: tcAgeCompare

config.prompt: 'The oldest manuscript is automatically the most faithful' — drag the divider to test it:

before.label: What the date alone says
before.text: A 4th-century copy must beat a 10th-century one — older is closer to the author.

after.label: What the descent says
after.text: A 10th-century copy made from an excellent 3rd-century book can beat a 4th-century copy that came down through a careless scribe — so editors weigh lineages, not dates alone, and one good new witness can overturn a century of consensus.

config.why: Distance from the author is measured along one copy's descent — and descent can be clean or careless at any date.

activities.anchor: group the copies by their mistakes
activities.caption: guess the magnitude before the reveal
activities.name: tcVariantsEstimate

config.prompt: The New Testament survives in roughly 5,800 Greek manuscripts — by Ehrman's count, roughly how many variants do they carry?
config.why: 200,000–400,000 variants, against about 140,000 words — the overwhelming majority trivial, a handful doctrinally loaded: the longer ending of Mark, the woman taken in adultery, the Comma Johanneum.
config.context: For scale: the book has about 140,000 words — more variants than words, by a factor of two or so.
